objectives: State the no-arbitrage principle + law of one price.
Price a forward contract by replication.
Define the risk-neutral measure + the FTAP.

slides.title: The no-arbitrage principle
slides.body:
**Arbitrage**: a riskless profit. A trading strategy with zero initial cost, no chance of loss, + positive chance of profit. In a well-functioning market, arbitrage doesn't exist (or vanishes within milliseconds as traders pile in).

**The no-arbitrage assumption** is THE foundational assumption of derivatives pricing. It's strong but defensible: if a security's price violates no-arbitrage, professionals will trade against it until prices align.

**Law of one price**: two cash-flow streams that pay the same in every state of the world must have the same price.

**Replication**: if a derivative's payoff can be exactly replicated by a portfolio of more-basic instruments, then by LOP the derivative's price = the replicating portfolio's cost.

**Example**: a 1-year forward contract on a non-dividend stock at price $K$. Payoff at expiry: $S_T - K$.

Replicating portfolio: buy 1 stock today (cost $S_0$); borrow $K e^{-rT}$ at risk-free rate (must repay $K$ at expiry). Net cash flow at expiry: own stock worth $S_T$, owe $K$. Net = $S_T - K$. Same payoff!

No-arbitrage forces forward price $F$ such that the cost of replication = 0:
$$F = S_0 e^{rT}$$

The entire field of derivatives pricing extends this template: replicate the payoff, compute the cost of replication.

slides.title: Risk-neutral measure + the FTAP
slides.body:
**The Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP)**: a market is arbitrage-free iff there exists a **risk-neutral probability measure** $\mathbb{Q}$ such that every asset's discounted price is a martingale under $\mathbb{Q}$.

In plainer terms: under $\mathbb{Q}$, every asset has expected return = risk-free rate $r$.
$$S_0 = e^{-rT} \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T]$$

This is NOT the real-world probability! In reality stocks have expected return higher than $r$ (the equity risk premium). The risk-neutral measure is a mathematical device that absorbs the risk premium into the probabilities themselves.

**Why this is useful**: option prices are
$$\text{price} = e^{-rT} \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\text{payoff}]$$
A call option's payoff is $\max(S_T - K, 0)$. Under $\mathbb{Q}$, this expectation is computable (e.g., Black-Scholes evaluates it in closed form when $S_T$ is log-normal under $\mathbb{Q}$).

**The completeness theorem (FTAP II)**: the market is complete (every payoff replicable) iff $\mathbb{Q}$ is UNIQUE. Black-Scholes models are complete. Stochastic-volatility + jump-diffusion models are typically incomplete (multiple valid $\mathbb{Q}$'s; each gives a different price).

Incompleteness means there's pricing discretion — you can hedge approximately, but not perfectly. Real markets are incomplete; banks add a margin to cover the hedging error.

slides.title: Put-call parity: a clean no-arbitrage example
slides.body:
Consider European call $C$ + put $P$ on the same stock, same strike $K$, same expiry $T$. Payoffs at expiry:
- Call: $\max(S_T - K, 0)$
- Put: $\max(K - S_T, 0)$
- Call − Put: $S_T - K$ (always, no matter $S_T$!)

This is exactly the payoff of a forward contract at $K$. Now no-arbitrage:
$$C - P = S_0 - K e^{-rT}$$

**Why useful**:
- Quick sanity check on quoted call + put prices: if they violate parity by more than transaction costs, arbitrage opportunity.
- Compute one from the other: given $C$ + market data, $P = C - S_0 + K e^{-rT}$.
- Synthesizes positions: long call + short put = long forward. Useful when one of the components is mis-priced or illiquid.

**Real markets**: parity holds to within bid-ask spreads in major equity index options. In single-name stocks, deviations can reflect borrow costs (shorting stock has a cost), dividends, hard-to-borrow situations. Sophisticated traders monitor parity deviations as an arbitrage / borrow-cost signal.

**Generalization**: every theoretical derivatives relationship is a no-arbitrage identity of this form. Mastering put-call parity (1 line of algebra) is the gateway to mastering more complex relations (American option early exercise, conversion / reversal trades, dispersion trades).

question.question: Derive the forward price by replication
question.goal: Forward contract on a non-dividend stock: deliver one stock for cash $F$ at time $T$. What is $F$ today?

steps.prompt: Long-forward payoff at $T$: $S_T - F$ (receive stock worth $S_T$, pay $F$). To replicate with stock + bond: buy how much stock today?
steps.motivation: We want to end up with one stock at $T$.
hints: We need to OWN 1 stock at expiry.
steps.reveal: Buy 1 stock today, hold until $T$. Cost: $S_0$.

steps.prompt: We owe $F$ at $T$. To replicate this debt, we should borrow how much today (so the loan matures to exactly $F$)?
steps.reveal: Borrow $F e^{-rT}$ today; it grows to $F$ at $T$.

steps.prompt: Net cost of the replicating portfolio today: $S_0 - F e^{-rT}$. Forward starts at zero cost (no money exchanges hands at $t=0$). Set equal to 0 + solve for $F$.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{F = S_0 e^{rT}}$$ The forward price on a non-dividend stock is the spot price compounded at the risk-free rate. If $F$ were higher: SELL the forward + BUY the stock with borrowed cash; risk-free profit. If $F$ were lower: BUY the forward + SHORT the stock + invest cash; risk-free profit. The single no-arbitrage condition pins $F$ exactly. Extending to dividend-paying stocks: $F = (S_0 - PV(\text{div})) e^{rT}$. Foreign exchange: $F = S_0 e^{(r_d - r_f)T}$ (covered interest parity).

question.question: A senior trader says 'the no-arbitrage assumption is wrong; real markets have arbitrages all the time'. What's the right way to think about this?
options: They're right; financial theory is broken.

Pure mathematical arbitrages are rare; small inefficiencies exist but are quickly closed by professionals (HFT). 'No-arbitrage' is a model assumption that's accurate at the timescales most pricing problems operate on.
Pure arbitrages are easy to find; you should look on Robinhood.
question.explanation: Real markets have transient inefficiencies measured in microseconds-to-minutes; HFT firms exist exactly to exploit + close them. By the time a retail trader sees a quote, professional liquidity providers have already arbitraged. For risk management + pricing models at second/day/longer horizons, no-arbitrage is a defensible approximation. The exceptions (closed-end fund discounts, illiquid markets, regulated FX pegs) are studied as special cases.

slides.workedSolution: HFT firms with co-located servers exploit microsecond mispricings. Stat-arb funds exploit minute/hour discrepancies. By the time deep liquidity is consumed, prices align. Pure 'free money' arbs essentially don't exist for retail. But model 'arbitrages' (mispricings relative to a SPECIFIC model) do exist — and exploiting them is the bread-and-butter of quant funds + market makers.

question.question: Given call $C = \$10$, stock $S_0 = \$100$, strike $K = \$95$, $r=5\%$, $T=1$. Put-call parity: $P = ?$
Why incomplete markets matter
question.prompt: Your firm trades options on illiquid single-name stocks. A senior PM says these are 'incomplete-market problems'. Explain what this means + how the firm should price + hedge given incompleteness.
Explain in two or three sentences why every derivative pricing model rests on the no-arbitrage assumption + replication argument.
question.rubric: Mentions that no-arbitrage forces prices to be self-consistent; replicating a payoff with simpler instruments lets us compute its price from instruments whose prices we know; the entire derivatives industry rests on this trick. Failure of replication (incomplete markets) is the source of pricing model uncertainty + bid-ask spreads.
